title: Local Variance-Based Calibration of Programmable Photonic Interferometer Meshes
authors: Gökhan Elmas, Igor A. Litvin, Janis Nötzel
abstract: Programmable photonic interferometer meshes enable reconfigurable linear optical transformations, but their performance depends critically on accurate calibration of Mach-Zehnder interferometers and phase shifters. Conventional methods often require node isolation, dedicated routing paths, orthogonal training states, reference channels, or prior phase-voltage characterization, which become increasingly difficult in large thermally tuned meshes.   We introduce a local variance-based self-calibration method using intensity-only measurements. Controlled phase perturbations are applied, and calibration points are identified from minima of the measured output-power variance. For Mach-Zehnder interferometers, the variance follows a characteristic |sin(theta)| dependence, allowing bar and cross operating points to be found without conventional node isolation. For phase shifters, balanced interference produces a complementary |cos(phi)| variance signature, enabling quadrature calibration through the same statistical principle.   We validate the method experimentally on an 8 x 8 silicon nitride programmable photonic processor using a fully automated two-stage procedure. Starting from random phase settings, all Mach-Zehnder interferometers are calibrated first, followed by phase-shifter calibration under balanced-interference conditions. As a system-level test, we implement an embedded 4 x 4 Hadamard transformation on the 8 x 8 processor using a Clements decomposition.   These results establish local output variance as a simple calibration observable for programmable photonic meshes. The method is compatible with discrete random phase ensembles and requires neither conventional node isolation nor orthogonal training fields, making it a practical calibration primitive for scalable self-stabilizing photonic processors.
summary: The paper presents a novel local variance-based method to self-calibrate programmable photonic interferometer meshes. By measuring the statistical variance of output intensity under controlled phase perturbations, the authors can accurately determine operating points for MZIs and phase shifters without needing complex node isolation or global training fields. This makes the technique highly practical for building scalable, self-stabilizing photonic processors.
main_problem: Accurately calibrating programmable photonic interferometer meshes is difficult using conventional methods due to requirements like node isolation or complex characterization procedures, especially in large, thermally tuned systems.
main_result: The authors introduce and validate a local variance-based self-calibration method that uses only intensity measurements to determine operating points for MZIs and phase shifters without requiring dedicated routing paths or orthogonal training states.
method: Calibration is achieved by applying controlled phase perturbations and identifying the calibration point from the minima of the measured output-power variance, which follows characteristic $|\sin 	heta|$ (for MZIs) or $|\cos \phi|$ (for PSs) dependencies.
model_or_system: The work focuses on programmable photonic interferometer meshes implemented on silicon nitride platforms, featuring Mach-Zehnder Interferometers (MZIs) and phase shifters arranged in large arrays (e.g., $8 	imes 8$ processors).
key_observables: Output-intensity variance ($	ext{Var}(P_{out})$), which exhibits characteristic $|\sin	heta|$ or $|\cos\phi|$ minima at operating points.
important_parameters: The method is robust to random phase settings and requires only a small, finite ensemble of measurements per calibration step.
main_assumptions: It assumes that local input fields are non-zero and that the variance observable can be used locally without needing global knowledge or perfect isolation between elements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup on an $8 	imes 8$ processor, showing theoretical signatures of the variance dependence for both MZIs ($|\sin	heta|$) and PSs ($|\cos\phi|$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of existing calibration techniques. It then derives the statistical relationship between output power variance and operating parameters ($\sigma(	heta) \propto |\sin 	heta|$, $\sigma(\phi) \propto |\cos \phi|$). Finally, it validates this method experimentally on a large processor using an automated two-stage procedure.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly practical, low-overhead calibration primitive for scalable integrated photonics, which is crucial for realizing complex quantum optical circuits and photonic quantum computing architectures.

Light from a continuous-wave laser is coupled into a selected input port through a polarization-maintaining fiber. The eight output ports are connected to individual photodetectors, whose electrical signals are digitized by an eight-channel analog-to-digital conversion stage and recorded on a computer. Blue lines denote optical fiber connections, whereas black lines denote electrical connections. Figure 2: Theoretical variance-based calibration signatures. (a) Normalized standard deviation of the monitored MZI output intensity as a function of the internal phase θ, showing the characteristic | sin θ| dependence. The minima at θ = 0 and θ = π identify the bar and cross operating points, respectively. (b) Normalized standard deviation of the phase-shifter calibration signal as a function of the phase-shifter phase ϕ under balanced-interference conditions, showing the characteristic | cos ϕ| dependence. The minima at ϕ = π/2 and ϕ = 3π/2 identify the quadrature operating points.

Figure 3: Experimental variance-based MZI calibration for MZI62. (a) Raw unnormalized output variance as a function of heater phase θ (unordered). (b) Same data after ordering. (c) Ordered and normalized variance following the theoretical | sin θ| dependence. (d) Extracted residual phase error ∆θ after calibration.

Figure 4: Experimental variance-based PS calibration for PS63. (a) Raw unnormalized output variance as a function of input phase ϕ (unordered). (b) Same data after ordering. (c) Ordered and normalized variance exhibiting the expected | cos ϕ| dependence with minima at quadrature. (d) Extracted residual phase error ∆θ after calibration.

Figure 5: System-level comparison between the manufacturer-provided factory calibration and the proposed variance-based calibration for an implemented 4×4 Hadamard transformation. The variance-based calibration yields more uniform output levels and reduced temporal fluctuations across the measured output channels.
